summary: Jumping worms are earthworms, up to 8 inches long with a metallic brown color, that thrash wildly when picked up. Unlike most earthworms, the pale band around their body lies flat instead of being raised. They eat the organic matter in soil that feeds native plants, leaving soil grainy and damaging plant roots, and heavy infestations have been linked to declines in native plants, soil invertebrates, salamanders and birds. Amynthas species are prohibited in New York State.
history: Jumping worms come from East Asia. They were brought to the southern United States in the late 1800s, likely on imported plants or horticultural materials.

handling.text: Prevention is the best tool. Don't buy or move jumping worms for composting, fishing or gardening, and avoid moving soil, mulch and plants from infested areas: their cocoons are smaller than a mustard seed and travel easily in soil and mulch. A single worm can start a new population, because they can reproduce without mating.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
